Yes, you're right, and it isn't pedantry because the two numbers can differ by a lot.

A p-value of 0.03 means that if the null were true, data this extreme or more would occur 3% of the time: P(data | H0). The claim "97% chance the hypothesis is true" is P(hypothesis | data), which also requires a prior and the power of the test. Also, 1 − p isn't the probability of anything about the hypothesis.

Two concrete illustrations:

- **Best case with an even prior:** the Sellke-Bayarri-Berger bound gives a minimum Bayes factor of about −e·p·ln(p) ≈ 0.29 for p = 0.03. That is at most ~3.5:1 evidence against the null, so with a 50/50 prior the alternative gets at most ~78%, not 97%. This is a heuristic bound, but it shows the gap.
- **Low prior:** if 10% of tested hypotheses are true and power is 80%, then among results significant at 0.05 about 36% are false positives.

If your colleague's version were roughly right, results at p ≈ 0.03 would replicate far more often than they do.
